walkthroughs.body_html:
Christianity through a Study of the Gospel of Matthew / Mark / Luke — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Christianity through a Study of the Gospel of Matthew / Mark / Luke brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Christianity through a Study of the Gospel of Matthew / Mark / Luke.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: In the Gospels, what is a parable?
options: A short everyday story teaching a spiritual truth
An eyewitness report of a miracle
A prayer recited in the synagogue
A law taken from the Old Testament

mcqs.q: Which of these is one of the Synoptic Gospels?
options: Mark
John
Acts
Revelation

mcqs.q: According to the Synoptic Gospels, what did Peter declare at Caesarea Philippi?
options: That Jesus is the Christ
That Jesus should be baptised
That the Temple would be rebuilt
That Rome should be overthrown by force

mcqs.q: At which event did Jesus share bread and wine with his disciples before his arrest?
options: The Last Supper
The Transfiguration
The feeding of the five thousand
The Sermon on the Mount
A parable is a type of psalm sung in the Temple.
Because they were the only Gospels accepted by the Roman Empire.
A short story from everyday life used by Jesus to teach a deeper spiritual truth, often about the Kingdom of God.
Parables are factual historical reports of events that actually happened.

mcqs.q: Why are Matthew, Mark and Luke called the Synoptic Gospels?
options: They are called synoptic because the same author wrote all three.
Because they share much of the same content, order and wording, so they can be 'seen together' (syn-optic) and compared side by side.
A parable is a type of psalm sung in the Temple.
Because they were the only Gospels accepted by the Roman Empire.

mcqs.q: What did Jesus teach about the Sabbath in the Synoptic Gospels?
options: Jesus taught that Sabbath laws must never be broken for any reason.
Because they were the only Gospels accepted by the Roman Empire.
Jesus abolished the idea of a day of rest entirely.
That 'the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath' (Mark 2:27) — human need, such as healing, takes priority over rigid observance.
